caption_hook: Florida is a limestone slab with a base from Africa, fossil reefs, shell-rock forts and bone beds.

layers.name: ANASTASIA FORMATION
layers.what: Tiny coquina clams piled up on ancient beaches and cemented into soft, speckled rock. Workers cut blocks of it on Anastasia Island to build St. Augustine's fort.
layers.bonus: Castillo de San Marcos shrugged off cannon fire because the soft shell rock absorbed it.

layers.name: KEY LARGO LIMESTONE
layers.hook: A fossil reef you can walk on
layers.what: When seas were higher between Ice Age glaciers, a coral reef grew along Florida's southern edge. That dead reef now forms the upper Florida Keys, with coral heads still visible.
layers.bonus: Windley Key's old railway quarry is now a state park with sawn walls full of fossil coral.

layers.name: BONE VALLEY FORMATION
layers.what: Phosphate-rich sand and clay near Tampa Bay are packed with the remains of sea creatures and land animals. Miners digging for fertilizer rock keep turning up shark teeth and whale bones.
layers.bonus: Florida mines most of America's phosphate, a key ingredient in crop fertilizer.

layers.name: OCALA LIMESTONE
layers.hook: The rock that holds Florida up
layers.what: Warm, shallow seas covered Florida, and countless tiny shelled creatures settled on the bottom. They hardened into limestone that now lies beneath much of the state.
layers.bonus: Water slowly dissolves it, carving Florida's famous springs, caves and sinkholes.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.hook: Florida began as part of Africa
layers.what: Thousands of feet below north Florida lie volcanic and granite rocks that match those of West Africa. Florida's foundation was left behind when the Atlantic Ocean opened.
layers.bonus: No one can see it: it is known only from deep drill holes and cores.
